requirements.requirement: /srv/drop exists as a shared, world-writable directory
requirements.summary: mkdir/chown/chmod 1777 applied; stat and ls -ld directly show '1777 root:root /srv/drop' and drwxrwxrwt permissions.

requirements.requirement: Users cannot remove files owned by other users (sticky-bit restricted deletion)
requirements.summary: testuser2's attempt to rm testuser1's file failed with 'Operation not permitted' and the file remained present; behavior re-verified after reboot with fresh files (file_from_user1_v2.txt).

requirements.requirement: Directory remains usable for normal write/delete-own-file operations
requirements.summary: testuser2 successfully created its own file and testuser1 successfully deleted its own file, confirming the directory isn't over-restricted.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol on node1 (pre-restart baseline, acknowledgement, changed boot identity, recovered config/data/behavior)
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id (d9f8550d...) and /srv/drop state captured, reboot acknowledged, outage observed via connection timeouts/reset, post-restart boot_id (b356d23e...) differs, and /srv/drop permissions, sticky-bit deny-delete behavior, and pre-existing file_from_user2.txt were confirmed intact afterward. Fixed global before_prepare/after_executor boot-identity observations independently corroborate the same boot_id transition.

overall_summary: The executor correctly configured /srv/drop with mode 1777 and root:root ownership, and directly demonstrated (via two test users) that cross-user deletion is denied while same-user creation/deletion and other-user creation work as expected. The mandated node-restart protocol was fully evidenced end-to-end: healthy pre-restart baseline, reboot acknowledgement, an observed outage window, a changed boot_id, and post-restart re-verification that the directory configuration, sticky-bit behavior, and pre-existing data survived. All material task outcomes are satisfied. The only deduction is operational hygiene: test users and several test/error files were left on the system rather than cleaned up after verification.
limitations: Test artifacts (testuser1, testuser2 accounts; file_from_user2.txt, file_from_user1_v2.txt in /srv/drop; /tmp/rm_err.txt, /tmp/rm_err2.txt) were not cleaned up, so the final state is not identical to a minimal clean configuration, though this does not affect functional correctness.

No packet/service-level evidence beyond boot_id and directory state was captured post-reboot (e.g., explicit sshd health check), though this is adequately inferred from the successful post-reboot commands.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands (mkdir/chown/chmod on /srv/drop, useradd for testuser1/testuser2, test file creates/deletes, sudo reboot) were directly tied to configuring or verifying the sticky-bit directory and the mandated restart protocol, so none were gratuitous experiments. However, residue was left behind and not cleaned up: two test accounts (testuser1, testuser2) remain on the system, leftover files file_from_user2.txt and file_from_user1_v2.txt persist inside /srv/drop, and stray error-capture files /tmp/rm_err.txt and /tmp/rm_err2.txt remain in /tmp, all visible in the after_executor temporary-files diff. These are low-risk, non-destructive artifacts but were never restored to the pre-task state, so hygiene is only partially clean.
